tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
schema.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). ---
name: feedback-ui-details-on-demand
description: Kenneth 2026-11-08 — I tend to assume users need every detail on screen; default to one summary line with details behind a disclosure
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Kenneth, 2026-11-08, on the JusPrin import result screen, where each skipped filament or print setting had its own row with a three-sentence reason: "You have a tendency of assuming that users need to know all the details." He proposed one general line saying some items weren't imported, with an expandable section or a tooltip for anyone who wants the specifics.

**Why:** most people only need to know the outcome and whether they must do anything. Per-item explanations crowd the screen and create their own misreadings. In this case, a reason row sitting in the printer list was taken for a failed printer.

**How to apply:** when designing JusPrin screens (and UI in general), put the outcome and any action in one short line and move per-item names and reasons behind a disclosure such as "Show details". Prefer an expandable section over a hover tooltip for anything longer than a few words. Before adding detail to the main view, ask whether a typical user would act differently because of it. Related: [[feedback-jusprin-canvas-read-guidelines-first]].

Yes, your approach is better, and you're right that I leaned toward showing everything. Think about someone who has just imported from OrcaSlicer. They mostly need three things: what came in, that a couple of items didn't, and whether they need to do anything. A three-sentence explanation for each skipped item answers a question most people won't ask. It also caused the problem the fresh reader hit: a long reason row sitting in the printer list looks like a printer that failed.

Here's what I'd draw:
- **One line under the list of imported items.** For example: "1 filament and 1 print setting weren't imported. They stay in OrcaSlicer." It names the kinds of items, so nobody mistakes them for printers. It says nothing is lost, which is the one fact that might worry someone.
- **A "Show details" link at the end of that line.** It opens an expandable section. For each skipped item, the section gives its name and the reason you approved: it's based on something JusPrin doesn't have, so choose a similar one when you prepare a print.

I'd use the expandable section rather than a tooltip, for three reasons:
- A tooltip only appears when you hover, so people don't know it's there.
- Keyboard users can't reach a tooltip.
- A tooltip handles a few words well but not several sentences.

This change also fixes a smaller problem the reader found. The screen before the import promises "3 print settings", and the result screen then says "2 of 3". With the new line, the skipped one is accounted for in plain words.

content.content:
1	# JusPrin design guidelines
2	
3	**Status:** Canonical guidance for `jusprin-newui` on how a screen gets designed and checked, and on the words it shows. The visual system (tokens, type, color, components, logo) lives in [Design system](design-system.md); this document does not repeat it.
4	
5	Design agents tend to write on-screen text that only they can read. The agent knows how the screen works, so a line like "The sixth digit signs you in." reads clearly to it and to any reviewer who knows the same. A person opening the app for the first time has to decode it, and often can't. The First-Launch Confusion Review (https://claude.ai/artifact/91wmdS3QU8UkzbPi1zog15, 2026-11-06) found 23 places on the first launch where a newcomer would misread or stall, and most of them were wording. The rules below exist to stop that at the source and to catch what still gets through.
6	
7	## How a screen gets designed and checked
8	
9	These steps apply to every change to text a person sees, not only to new screens: a new link on an existing board, a reworded line, or a one-sentence fix all get the cold-reader check on the board before building (step 5) and in the running app after (step 8).
10	
11	1. **Start from the person.** Before drawing, write down in two or three sentences who reaches this screen, what they know at that moment, what they came to do, and what they must decide here. Every line on the screen serves one of those.
12	2. **Draw the whole screen, not a component alone.** A board for review is the full screen at the app's size, with the header, panes and neighbouring content the person really sees there, on the JusPrin v2 canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ). Build it from the Design System artifact's coded components and the app's own markup, never by copying an older board. Repeated compositions are imported by name, as [Design handoff requirements](design-system.md#design-handoff-requirements) rule 9 says.
13	3. **Fill it with real strings.** Text that summarises data comes from the rule that will produce it in the app, run on real data. If only a model could write a line, say so on the board.
14	4. **Write every line by the wording rule below.**
15	5. **Run the cold-reader check on the boards** (below). Rewrite and check again until every line and button reads as intended.
16	6. **Show the board for review by what a person sees.** Name the screen as the person would ("the welcome screen, after typing an email"), give the canvas page it is on, and attach the picture. Board ids and builder labels mean nothing to a reviewer.
17	7. **Build it** following [Writing UI code](design-system.md#writing-ui-code).
18	8. **Check it in the running app.** Take screenshots of the built screen along one real path and run the cold-reader check again. The guards prove the code went through the tokens; only the screenshots show what the person reads.
19	
20	## The cold-reader check
21	
22	The writer of a screen cannot see that its text is cryptic, so the check is done by a reader who knows nothing about how the screen works.
23	
24	- Start a fresh agent. Give it only the screenshots and one or two sentences a real user would know (for example: "You own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin, a desktop app that prepares 3D models for printing."). Give it no code, spec, design notes, chat history or list of suspected problems, and rename files so their names don't hint at anything.
25	- Use screenshots from one coherent path, in the order a person meets them. Mixing signed-in and signed-out screens, or states set by hand, makes the reader report contradictions that no user would see.
26	- Ask it, for each screen, to quote every line and every button exactly, say in one plain sentence what the line means or what the button will do, and list where it would hesitate, misread, worry, or not know what to do next, including information the screen leaves out. Tell it to read literally, like a busy newcomer: a line it had to puzzle out counts as a problem even if it worked it out.
27	- Compare its answers with the intent written in step 1. Any line it reads differently from the intent gets rewritten, however small the gap. Its other hesitations are input to weigh, not orders.
28

# JusPrin design guidelines

**Status:** Canonical guidance for `jusprin-newui` on how a screen gets designed and checked, and on the words it shows. The visual system (tokens, type, color, components, logo) lives in [Design system](design-system.md); this document does not repeat it.

Design agents tend to write on-screen text that only they can read. The agent knows how the screen works, so a line like "The sixth digit signs you in." reads clearly to it and to any reviewer who knows the same. A person opening the app for the first time has to decode it, and often can't. The First-Launch Confusion Review (https://claude.ai/artifact/91wmdS3QU8UkzbPi1zog15, 2026-11-06) found 23 places on the first launch where a newcomer would misread or stall, and most of them were wording. The rules below exist to stop that at the source and to catch what still gets through.

## How a screen gets designed and checked

These steps apply to every change to text a person sees, not only to new screens: a new link on an existing board, a reworded line, or a one-sentence fix all get the cold-reader check on the board before building (step 5) and in the running app after (step 8).

1. **Start from the person.** Before drawing, write down in two or three sentences who reaches this screen, what they know at that moment, what they came to do, and what they must decide here. Every line on the screen serves one of those.
2. **Draw the whole screen, not a component alone.** A board for review is the full screen at the app's size, with the header, panes and neighbouring content the person really sees there, on the JusPrin v2 canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ). Build it from the Design System artifact's coded components and the app's own markup, never by copying an older board. Repeated compositions are imported by name, as [Design handoff requirements](design-system.md#design-handoff-requirements) rule 9 says.
3. **Fill it with real strings.** Text that summarises data comes from the rule that will produce it in the app, run on real data. If only a model could write a line, say so on the board.
4. **Write every line by the wording rule below.**
5. **Run the cold-reader check on the boards** (below). Rewrite and check again until every line and button reads as intended.
6. **Show the board for review by what a person sees.** Name the screen as the person would ("the welcome screen, after typing an email"), give the canvas page it is on, and attach the picture. Board ids and builder labels mean nothing to a reviewer.
7. **Build it** following [Writing UI code](design-system.md#writing-ui-code).
8. **Check it in the running app.** Take screenshots of the built screen along one real path and run the cold-reader check again. The guards prove the code went through the tokens; only the screenshots show what the person reads.

## The cold-reader check

The writer of a screen cannot see that its text is cryptic, so the check is done by a reader who knows nothing about how the screen works.

- Start a fresh agent. Give it only the screenshots and one or two sentences a real user would know (for example: "You own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin, a desktop app that prepares 3D models for printing."). Give it no code, spec, design notes, chat history or list of suspected problems, and rename files so their names don't hint at anything.
- Use screenshots from one coherent path, in the order a person meets them. Mixing signed-in and signed-out screens, or states set by hand, makes the reader report contradictions that no user would see.
- Ask it, for each screen, to quote every line and every button exactly, say in one plain sentence what the line means or what the button will do, and list where it would hesitate, misread, worry, or not know what to do next, including information the screen leaves out. Tell it to read literally, like a busy newcomer: a line it had to puzzle out counts as a problem even if it worked it out.
- Compare its answers with the intent written in step 1. Any line it reads differently from the intent gets rewritten, however small the gap. Its other hesitations are input to weigh, not orders.

What the check is known to catch: on 2026-11-06 a fresh agent given only the review's ten screenshots fully caught 14 of the 23 problems and partly caught 4 more. It caught every cryptic phrasing in the list. It missed problems that need knowledge from outside the screen (that Skip installs a 250 mm Klipper printer) and finer editorial calls (a redundant reassurance, one allowance under three names, "Connected" used for an account). It also raised real questions the review had not, such as what happens after the free month. It has not been compared with a real first-time user, so for the screens that matter most, such as first launch, a person remains the final test.

## Wording

Every line says what the person does or what happens to them, in a full sentence, in words a newcomer already has.

The five patterns below are what the review found most. Each pair is the text the app showed and the review's proposed rewrite; the rewrites are proposals, not yet in the app.

1. **Facts joined by a middle dot.** The dot drops how the facts relate, and the reader guesses.
   - Before: "Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits" (reads like a balance the person already had)
   - After: "You got 500 free credits for signing up.", with the email address on a smaller line under it
2. **Metaphors.** The reader has to work out what the image stands for.
   - Before: "New or existing account, same door."
   - After: a "Sign up free" button, with "Already have an account? Sign in" under it
   - Before: "Pick how the agent should think." (the options are ways to pay for or connect the agent)
   - After: "Sign up to use the AI agent, or skip it and just slice."
3. **Describing the mechanism instead of the action.** Say what the person does, not how the screen works inside.
   - Before: "The sixth digit signs you in. Read the email on any device."
   - After: "Type the code from the email. You can open it on your phone."
4. **Internal labels.** A name the team uses, shown nowhere else on the screen, explains nothing.
   - Before: "An Expert message is 5 credits."
   - After: the cost in things the person does, for example "500 credits is about 100 questions to the agent" (check the number against real costs)
5. **Hinting at a consequence instead of stating it.** If a choice changes what the person gets, say what it changes.
   - Before: "Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours."
   - After: "If you skip, files are sliced for a stand-in printer with a 250 mm bed, not for yours. Add your printer before you print anything. You can do that later on the home screen."

Space on a screen is tight, and short text looks finished. That is how these lines get written. Shorten only after the full sentence passes the cold-reader check, and check again after shortening.

"""Screenshot canvas boards with headless Chrome. Usage: render.py <canvas project dir> <out dir> <board.dc.html>..."""
import json, re, shutil, subprocess, sys
from pathlib import Path
proj, out = Path(sys.argv[1]), Path(sys.argv[2])
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
(out / 'fonts').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for f in Path('/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/WebShared/fonts').glob('HarmonyOS_Sans_SC_*_latin.woff'):
    shutil.copy(f, out / 'fonts' / f.name)
shutil.copy(proj / 'ds/jusprin/tokens.css', out / 'tokens.css')

boards = json.loads((proj / 'canvas.json').read_text())['boards']
chrome = '/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome'
for name in sys.argv[3:]:
    s = (proj / name).read_text()
    body = s[s.index('</helmet>') + 9:s.index('</x-dc>')]
    m = re.search(r'"\$preview":\{"width":(\d+),"height":(\d+)\}', s)
    w, h = (int(m.group(1)), int(m.group(2))) if m else (boards[name]['w'], boards[name]['h'])
    page = out / (name + '.html')
    page.write_text(f'<!doctype html><html><head><meta charset="utf-8"><link rel="stylesheet" href="tokens.css"><style>body{{margin:0}}</style></head><body>{body}</body></html>')
    png = out / (name.replace('.dc.html', '') + '.png')
    subprocess.run([chrome, '--headless=new', '--disable-gpu', '--no-first-run', '--user-data-dir=/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-claude-cowork-wd/24e670f8-e6ad-4332-8afd-c75ed03c29c0/scratchpad/render-profile', '--hide-scrollbars', f'--window-size={w},{h}', '--force-device-scale-factor=1',
                    f'--screenshot={png}', page.as_uri()], check=True, capture_output=True, timeout=60)
    print(png)

## Screen 1: offer to bring printers over from OrcaSlicer

| Exact text | What I take it to mean |
|---|---|
| "You got 500 free credits for signing up, good until 6 December." | I have 500 credits to spend on something before 6 December. |
| "Signed in as alex@example.com" | This is the account I'm logged in with. |
| "Bring your printers from OrcaSlicer?" | JusPrin is offering to copy my printers over from OrcaSlicer. |
| "JusPrin copies these printers with their filaments, settings and printer connections. OrcaSlicer keeps its own copy." | It copies the printers and their related setup, and nothing is removed from OrcaSlicer. |
| [checked] "Bambu Lab P1S 0.4 nozzle" / [checked] "Prusa MK4 0.4 nozzle" / [checked] "Creality K1C 0.4 nozzle" | These are my three OrcaSlicer printers, and all are selected for copying. |
| "Also brings 3 filaments and 2 print settings." | Five more items come along with the printers. |
| "OrcaSlicer keeps these in ~/Library/Application Support/OrcaSlicer" | This is the folder JusPrin found them in. |
| "JusPrin starts with Bambu Lab P1S 0.4 nozzle, the printer OrcaSlicer had selected." | My active printer in JusPrin will be the P1S, the same one I had picked in OrcaSlicer. |
| Button "Import" | It copies the checked printers and their extras. |
| "Other ways:" "Import from JusPrin 1…" | It brings settings from an older JusPrin, which I've never used. |
| "Choose my printer" | It skips the import and lets me pick a printer from a list. |
| "Back" | It goes back to the previous step. |

Where I'd hesitate:
1. **Credits.** I don't know what credits are for, or how far 500 goes. I also wonder whether pressing Import spends any of them.
2. **"their filaments".** It reads as if filaments belong to a printer. I had to puzzle out that it means the filaments I use with them.
3. **"settings".** It doesn't say which settings. The next line calls them "print settings", so I suspect they're the same thing, but I'm not sure.
4. **"printer connections".** Does this mean JusPrin will connect to my printers itself? With the Bambu, I'd worry that JusPrin and OrcaSlicer would fight over the same printer, or that my access code gets copied somewhere.
5. **"3 filaments and 2 print settings" are not named.** I can't see which ones they are or choose among them. I also can't tell whether unchecking a printer changes what comes along.
6. **The folder path line.** It's a technical path, and I don't know why I'm being told it. I can't tell whether "these" means the printers or the filaments and print settings. The folder icon makes it look clickable, but I don't know if it is.
7. **The P1S starting line.** What happens if I uncheck the P1S? The screen doesn't say.
8. **"Import from JusPrin 1…"** The text is cut off. It also makes me wonder whether there's a JusPrin 1 I was supposed to install first.
9. **"Choose my printer".** It isn't clear that this is the way to skip the import.
10. **"Back".** I don't know what's behind it. I'd worry it signs me out.
11. **Things the screen leaves out:**
    - Whether my own tweaks come over, or only the stock profiles.
    - Whether later changes in OrcaSlicer will sync to JusPrin.
    - Whether I can run the import again later.

## Screen 2: after pressing Import

| Exact text | What I take it to mean |
|---|---|
| "Imported from OrcaSlicer" | The import is done. |
| "Bambu Lab P1S 0.4 nozzle" "Imported" (same for "Prusa MK4 0.4 nozzle" and "Creality K1C 0.4 nozzle") | Each printer was copied successfully. |
| "Also imported: 2 filaments (Generic PLA, Elegoo PETG) and 2 print settings (0.12mm Fine, 0.28mm Draft)." | These are the extras that came across. |
| "1 filament wasn't imported. It stays in OrcaSlicer." | One filament didn't come over, but it is still safe in OrcaSlicer. |
| Link "Show details" | It shows which filament failed and why. |
| Button "Continue" | It moves me on to the app. |

Where I'd hesitate:
1. **3 versus 2 filaments.** Screen 1 promised three, and this screen says two. I noticed the gap before I read the warning line.
2. **The warning doesn't say which filament or why.** I have to click to find out, and it doesn't say whether I need to act.
3. **"It stays in OrcaSlicer."** This is reassuring that nothing was deleted, but it hints that I'd have to go back to OrcaSlicer to use it.
4. **Printer connections are never mentioned.** Screen 1 promised them, and this screen is silent. I can't tell whether JusPrin can actually send a print to my printers.
5. **Nothing confirms the P1S is now the active printer.**
6. **Are these my versions?** I can't tell whether "0.12mm Fine" and "0.28mm Draft" are my customised versions or the stock ones.

## Screen 3: after clicking "Show details"

| Exact text | What I take it to mean |
|---|---|
| Link "Hide details" | It collapses the explanation again. |
| "My Silk PLA" | This is the filament that wasn't imported. It's my own custom one. |
| "It's based on Kingroon PLA Silk, which JusPrin doesn't have. When you prepare a print, choose a similar filament instead." | JusPrin lacks the profile mine was built on, so it couldn't copy my version. I should pick something close instead. |
| Button "Continue" | Same as before: it moves me on to the app. |

Where I'd hesitate:
1. **"choose a similar filament".** It doesn't say which one counts as similar. Generic PLA seems likely, but that would lose silk-specific settings.
2. **My custom values may be lost.** My temperatures and flow tweaks for My Silk PLA are apparently not carried over. The screen doesn't offer to recreate them, or show me what they were.
3. **"When you prepare a print".** It reads as if I have to remember this every time. I can't tell whether JusPrin will remind me or pick the substitute itself.
4. **I didn't know the base profile.** I may not have known My Silk PLA was based on Kingroon PLA Silk, so I had to puzzle out why that mattered.
5. **Why is the profile missing?** OrcaSlicer has the Kingroon profile and JusPrin doesn't. I'd wonder whether it might be added later and the import retried.
6. **Things the screen leaves out:**
    - A way to create the filament now.
    - A way to try the import again.

## What I believe happened

All three printers, two filaments and two print settings were copied into JusPrin, and nothing in OrcaSlicer was changed or removed. My Silk PLA did not come over. I think I'll need to pick a substitute such as Generic PLA, or re-enter my silk settings myself, whenever I print with it. I'm not sure whether JusPrin can actually talk to my printers yet, because "printer connections" were promised on the first screen and never confirmed afterwards.</result>

3. **"settings".** It doesn't say which settings. The next line calls them "print settings", so I suspect they're the same thing, but I'm not sure.
4. **"printer connections".** Does this mean JusPrin will connect to my printers itself? With the Bambu, I'd worry that JusPrin and OrcaSlicer would fight over the same printer, or that my access code gets copied somewhere.
5. **"3 filaments and 2 print settings" are not named.** I can't see which ones they are or choose among them. I also can't tell whether unchecking a printer changes what comes along.

Where I'd hesitate:

- `4-file-import-result-collapsed.jpg` and `5-file-import-result-details-open.jpg`: File › Import, the result with details closed and open

- **"Show details" / "Hide details":** both expected it to show which items and why.
- **Each item's reason:** both read the "It's based on …" sentences as "skipped because its base is missing; pick something similar when you print". Both called "based on" jargon, and both wanted a way to fix or retry.

**Not changed:**
- **Kingroon contradiction:** both readers saw "Kingroon PLA Silk @Qidi…" imported, then read "based on Kingroon PLA Silk, which JusPrin doesn't have". I caused this by naming my test filament's base after one already in the test folder. A real folder rarely holds both names, so I left the wording alone.
- **"New filament" before importing:** in File › Import, the screen before importing lists the two skipped items as "New filament" and "New print settings", and they then fail. That is the existing rule that counts an item as new while a new printer is on offer. I didn't change that screen, and it keeps the long "Not imported, because…" sentence.
- **My own additions:** a skipped printer counts as "1 printer" in the warning line; the brief gave only filament and print-setting wording. Reasons other than a missing base, such as "JusPrin couldn't read this file…", show unchanged under the item's name.
- **Apostrophes:** the reasons under each name use straight apostrophes, as the C++ file does. The line above them uses curly ones.

Background: the first-launch OrcaSlicer import screen says "JusPrin copies these printers with their filaments, print settings and printer connections." Nobody has checked the importer code (OrcaImporter.cpp and related files on ui-walkthrough) for what it does with connection settings (host, API key or access code).

Two possible fixes, depending on what you find:
- If connections are imported: say so briefly on the result screen, for example "Imported, with its connection" on a printer's row.
- If they aren't: remove the promise from the first-launch screen.

Either one is a text change, so it follows the design guideline: redraw the board first, run the cold-reader check, and get Kenneth's approval before building. Remember his preference for details on demand: keep any confirmation to a few words.

content.text:
You're right on both counts, and my earlier answer was wrong. The rule was removed: commit b0a2fe3b08, on 2026-11-06, deleted the "Landing a branch on jusprin-newui" section from AGENTS.md. Neither `jusprin-newui` nor `ui-walkthrough` has it today. I quoted the commit that added the rule without checking the current file.

**What the 22 commits cover** (the ones on `ui-walkthrough` that aren't on `jusprin-newui`). Almost all of it is the first-launch experience and what hangs off it:
- **First launch and importing printers (14 commits):** finding OrcaSlicer and JusPrin 1, the three ways to set up a printer, the import window and result screen, and today's wording.
- **Plan and billing (2 commits):** See prices on the welcome screen, the server's pricing pages in an in-app sheet, "+N credits" after buying, Delete account.
- **Account and sign-in (4 commits):** sign-in with the first-launch form everywhere, the Account box in Preferences, "No plan", and the Bring Your Own AI section in Preferences.
- **Design guideline notes (2 commits):** when to run the cold-reader check, and updating boards before code.

So squashing them into one commit makes sense. The simplest way is `git merge --squash ui-walkthrough` when landing on `jusprin-newui`. That makes one commit there without rewriting or force-pushing `ui-walkthrough`. Two things to know:
- **Timing:** the printer-setup session is still building the removal of the "JusPrin starts with…" line, so the squash should wait until that's pushed.
- **Branches will look unmerged:** git will show the session branches that went into `ui-walkthrough` as unmerged. That only matters if those sessions keep working on them.

`jusprin-newui` also has 2 newer commits, including the upstream-merge note. The squash merge brings those together with this work.

**Decision needed:** should I land `ui-walkthrough` on `jusprin-newui` as one squashed commit once the current build is pushed? It means running the tests on the result and pushing `jusprin-newui`, which is the branch everyone builds from. The other option is to wait, if more first-launch changes are coming. My pick is to land it once the build is in.

First launch, printer import, plan and billing, and account: the reviewed walkthrough

Everything a new person meets on the first launch of JusPrin 2, reworked
after Kenneth's walkthrough and cold-reader checks, as one change.

- Printers step: three ways to set up printers (import from OrcaSlicer,
  import from JusPrin 1, or choose a printer by hand). OrcaSlicer and
  JusPrin 1 are found in their real folders, and JusPrin 1 is imported the
  same way as OrcaSlicer: printers, presets and connections, not its
  settings.
- Import window and result: each printer chosen before importing; new
  filaments and print settings listed as rows; "nothing to import" when
  nothing can be. After importing, the box lists only the printers, an
  "Also imported" line names the rest, and one line counts what wasn't
  imported, with each item's reason behind "Show details". The screens no
  longer promise printer connections or name the printer JusPrin starts
  with.

  an in-app sheet, "+N credits" after buying, Billing and usage and Delete
  account in Account.
- Account and sign-in: the first-launch sign-in form everywhere
  (Preferences › Account, Home, the welcome-back window), "No plan" and
  "AI unavailable" states, and Bring Your Own AI in Preferences for your
  own keys and AI tools.
- Wording: the sign-up offer, the AI's name, settings menus and a sweep of
  on-screen text, rewritten to the design guideline.
- Design guideline: boards change before code, and every on-screen text
  change gets the cold-reader check on the board and in the built app.

EOF
